usage: The standard polite invitation at a door; warmer than the bare command 들어와요.
에 marks the place entered; in daily life this is the normal way to say 'get home'.
으로 marks direction; 안 (inside) makes the 'into here' clear when it is cold or raining.
Figurative: news, calls, or orders 'come in' to you — note the subject takes 이/가, not 를.
examples: 빨리 들어와.
Come in, quick.
Bare 들어와 (반말) to a close friend or family at the door.
집에 몇 시에 들어와요?
What time do you get home?
Everyday register; 들어오다 is the natural verb for arriving home, not 오다.
아까 회사로 주문이 많이 들어왔어요.
A lot of orders came in to the office earlier.
Real-situation, figurative use: 주문이 들어오다 = orders come in (subject + 이/가).
nuance: 들어오다 combines 들다 (to enter) + 오다 (to come), so it is specifically 'to come IN toward where the speaker/hearer is'. The hard contrast for English speakers is its twin 들어가다 (들다 + 가다): both translate as 'go/come in', but Korean forces you to track viewpoint — choose 들어오다 only when the motion is toward your side, and 들어가다 when it moves away. In daily life 집에 들어오다 means 'get home' (not just 오다), and it also goes figurative for things arriving to you: 연락/전화/주문/돈이 들어오다, where the subject takes 이/가, never 를. Politeness ranges from the blunt 들어와 to the welcoming 들어오세요 you say to a guest. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 들어가요 the way English reuses 'come', and forgetting that 'inside here' wants 안으로/안에.

mistakes: Saying 들어가요 when you mean entering toward yourself — English 'come in' maps to 들어와요; 들어가다 moves away from you.
Marking incoming messages with 를: write 연락이 들어왔어요, not 연락을 들어왔어요 — this 들어오다 is intransitive.
Using 오다 alone for arriving home (집에 와요) when Koreans naturally say 집에 들어와요 for getting home for the day.

usage: The destination takes 으로/로 (toward), not 에 — this is the core pattern.
With 를/을 it shifts to 'face/be oriented toward' rather than physically travel.
향해 (the 어-form) acts adverbially: '…를 향해' = aiming toward, then a motion verb.
Figurative, slightly literary: striving toward a goal — common in speeches and songs.
examples: 우리는 공항으로 향했어요.
We headed for the airport.
Simple: destination 공항 + 으로 = toward.
차가 북쪽을 향해 달렸어요.
The car raced northward.
Everyday: '…를 향해' + a motion verb pins down the facing direction.
발표가 끝나고 모두 출구로 향하고 있어요.
After the talk everyone is heading for the exit.
Real-situation; -고 있다 = in progress, slightly formal narration style.
nuance: 향하다 is Sino-Korean: 向 ('turn toward, face') + 하다, literally 'to do facing'. It means to head for or be oriented toward a direction/destination, which is marked with 으로/로 (집으로 향하다); when it takes 를/을 it leans toward 'to face' (바다를 향하다). The synonym line versus plain 가다: 가다 just says you move, while 향하다 spotlights the direction you are aimed at, and it reads more formal or written — in casual speech people simply say 집에 가요, not 집으로 향해요. A very common shape is the 어-form 향해 used adverbially: '…를/으로 향해 + motion verb' (출구를 향해 걸어가다). It also goes figurative — 꿈/목표를 향해 나아가다 — sounding aspirational. The English-speaker pitfall is forcing 에 ('to a place') as in '집에 향해요'; 향하다 wants 으로/로, and overusing it in everyday chat sounds stiff.

Dropping the object marker before 향해: it is 바다를 향해, not 바다 향해, when expressing 'facing the sea'.

usage: 에 marks the place of stay; the classic travel/lodging collocation.
Duration sits bare before the verb: 며칠/일주일 머물다 (no particle on the span).
잠시·잠깐 머물다 stresses a short stop; can be a physical pause or a gaze lingering.
Figurative: a memory or feeling 'stays'; gentle, slightly literary tone.
examples: 서울에 며칠 머물러요.
I'm staying in Seoul for a few days.
Simple; 며칠 (a few days) sits with no particle.
이번 출장 때는 친구 집에 머물렀어요.
This business trip I stayed at a friend's place.
Everyday; note the 어-form past 머물렀어요 (double 러).
관광객들이 보통 일주일쯤 머뭅니다.
Tourists usually stay about a week.
Real-situation, formal 합쇼체: the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다 → 머뭅니다.
nuance: 머물다 means to stay or remain somewhere for a stretch of time — a hotel, a friend's house, a city — and figuratively for a feeling or gaze that lingers (마음에 머물다). It is a ㄹ-stem (ㄹ-탈락) verb, the trap that trips up English speakers most: the ㄹ silently drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, giving 머뭅니다 and the polite request 머무세요, while the 어-form irregularly doubles to 머물러요 / 머물렀어요. The synonym boundary: 묵다 is the close cousin specifically for lodging overnight (호텔에서 묵다) and feels a touch more colloquial for 'put up at'; 있다 ('be/stay') is what casual travel talk actually uses — 호텔에 있어요 — while 머물다 sounds a bit more composed or written. Place takes 에, and a duration like 며칠 or 일주일 sits bare with no particle. The pitfall is regularizing the conjugation: not 머물습니다 and not 머물어요.

Putting a particle on the duration: say 며칠 머물러요, not 며칠을 머물러요 — the time span stands bare.

usage: 가까이 (closely) reinforces the 'nearer toward me' sense of the verb.
The person approached takes 한테(casual)/에게(formal), the goal of the motion.
Time/events as subject (이/가): a date 'approaches' — a very natural figurative use.
Figurative: words or art 'come close to' the heart, i.e. feel touching.
examples: 강아지가 저한테 다가왔어요.
The puppy came up to me.
Simple; 한테 marks me as the point it moved toward.
조금만 더 다가와 봐.
Come just a little closer.
Everyday 반말 with -아 보다 (try doing); said to a friend for a photo.
시험 날짜가 점점 다가오니까 더 떨려요.
As the exam date keeps approaching, I'm more nervous.
Real-situation, figurative: 날짜가 다가오다 (subject + 이/가), -니까 = since.
nuance: 다가오다 is 다가서다/다가- ('draw near') + 오다 (come), so it is 'to approach TOWARD the speaker' — a person, animal, or even a date getting closer. The viewpoint contrast English speakers must internalize is its mirror verb 다가가다 (… + 가다): identical meaning but opposite direction, so 다가오다 = it nears me, 다가가다 = I near it. Versus the simpler 가까워지다 ('become close', often abstract like relationships), 다가오다 keeps a sense of active motion or a looming approach. A person you approach takes 한테/에게; when time or events are the subject they take 이/가 (시험이 다가와요) and the verb becomes the go-to way to say something is 'coming up'. It can also mean 'resonate' — 마음에 다가오다. The pitfall is mixing the come/go pair, plus marking the approaching event with 를 instead of 이/가.

Marking the looming event with 를: it is 시험이 다가와요, not 시험을 다가와요 — the event is the subject.
Using the person as a 를-object: a person approached takes 한테/에게 (저한테 다가왔어요), not 저를 다가왔어요.

usage: The target person takes 한테/에게; you move toward someone away from the speaker.
천천히·조심해서 pair naturally when you near something timid or fragile.
으로/로 marks the direction or object you close in on (창문으로 다가가다).
Figurative business use: 'connect with / get closer to' people emotionally.
examples: 고양이한테 천천히 다가갔어요.
I slowly approached the cat.
Simple; 한테 + 천천히 — moving toward the cat (away from me).
그 사람한테 먼저 다가가 보세요.
Try reaching out to that person first.
Everyday advice; -아 보다 (give it a try) + 먼저 (first).
그 브랜드는 젊은 세대에게 더 가까이 다가가려고 해요.
That brand is trying to connect more closely with the younger generation.
Real-situation, figurative; -려고 하다 = intend to, 에게 marks the audience.
nuance: 다가가다 is 다가- ('draw near') + 가다 (go), the 'going' counterpart of 다가오다: you move closer toward a target that sits away from the speaker. The whole difficulty for English speakers is that English 'approach' has no built-in direction, but Korean splits it by viewpoint — 다가가다 = I close in on it, 다가오다 = it closes in on me — so you must pick based on where 'here' is. The destination/person takes 으로/로 or 한테/에게, never 를 (you don't 'approach-transitive' it). Beyond physical motion it is heavily used figuratively for emotional outreach — 고객에게/사람에게 다가가다 = to connect with, win over, get close to people — which a marketing or self-help context will use constantly. Contrast 가까워지다, which describes the resulting closeness/relationship rather than the act of moving in. The pitfall is reversing the come/go pair and slapping 를 on the goal.

mistakes: Using 다가가다 when something moves toward you — that is 다가오다; this verb moves you toward a target.
Marking the target with 를: say 창문으로 다가가요 or 그 사람한테 다가가요, not 창문을/그 사람을 다가가요.
Assuming it is only physical — for 'reach out to / connect with people' 다가가다 is the idiomatic choice (고객에게 다가가다).

usage: The set leaving-home phrase with -ㄹ게요 (I will, with intent to return).
The standard reply to someone heading out; literally 'go and come back (please)'.
잘 다녀오다 = have a safe round trip; 여행 잘 다녀왔어요? after a trip.
Formal 합쇼체 version, e.g. to a boss or in the military before stepping out.
examples: 학교 다녀올게요.
Off to school — back later!
Simple; the everyday line a student says leaving the house.
잠깐 화장실 다녀올게요.
I'll just pop to the restroom.
Everyday; the polite way to step away briefly and signal you'll return.
부모님 댁에 다녀오느라 주말이 다 갔어요.
Visiting my parents' place ate up the whole weekend.
Real-situation; -느라 = because (doing), 댁 = honorific 'home'.
nuance: 다녀오다 is 다니다 ('go to and fro, frequent') + 오다 (come), fusing 'go AND come back' into one verb — so it is the natural choice whenever you leave somewhere but will return. This is a concept English lacks a single word for, which is exactly the pitfall: learners say plain 가다, but 가요 implies departing (maybe for good), whereas 다녀올게요 promises a round trip. It anchors two everyday home rituals: the person leaving says 다녀올게요 / 다녀오겠습니다, and whoever stays answers 다녀오세요 — a tiny exchange you will hear in every Korean household and drama. Compare 갔다 오다, which is the more casual, separable 'went and came back' (잠깐 갔다 올게); 다녀오다 is a touch tidier and also covers regular attendance (학교/회사에 다녀오다). Place takes 에 (or is dropped in 학교 다녀올게요). The trap is using a goodbye like 잘 가 here — that is for the one staying to say to the one leaving for good.

usage: 에 marks the place; spotlights the very moment of crossing the threshold.
으로 marks direction; 안으로 들어서다 = cross into the interior.
들어서다 loves -자/-니 clauses: 방에 들어서자 (the instant I stepped in) …
Figurative: a society/economy 'enters' a phase — common in news writing.
examples: 문을 열고 안에 들어섰어요.
I opened the door and stepped inside.
Simple; pairs with 문을 열고 (opening the door) to mark the act of entering.
방에 들어서니 따뜻한 공기가 확 느껴졌어요.
The moment I stepped into the room, warm air hit me.
Everyday; -니 = as/when, capturing the instant of crossing in.
한국 경제가 새로운 국면에 들어섰습니다.
The Korean economy has entered a new phase.
Real-situation, figurative; formal news register with 국면에 들어서다.
nuance: 들어서다 is 들다 (enter) + 서다 (stand/step), so its core image is 'to step across and stand inside' — it pinpoints the moment of crossing the threshold, not the journey of entering. The contrast English speakers need is with 들어가다/들어오다: those track direction (in-away vs in-toward), whereas 들어서다 freezes the instant your foot lands inside, which is why it pairs so often with -자/-니 ('the moment I stepped in …'). It is slightly more descriptive/literary, so for plain spoken 'go in / come in' a beginner should still reach for 들어가다 and 들어오다. It also has a strong figurative life in writing: 새 시대/국면/단계에 들어서다 = to enter a new era/phase/stage, and 건물이 들어서다 = a building 'goes up/comes to stand' on a site. Place takes 에, direction 으로. The pitfall is treating it as a free synonym of 들어가다 in casual speech, where it sounds oddly narrated.

Missing its idiomatic figurative use — 새 시대에 들어서다 (enter a new era) is standard; a flat 들어가다 there feels off.

english: to go over / to pass over
usage: to move on to the next
으로 marks the next item/step; the everyday 'let's move on' of classes and meetings.
를/을 marks the obstacle crossed; literal 'over and to the other side'.
to let it slide / let it go
Idiomatic: 그냥 넘어가다 = overlook it without making an issue.
Set phrase for sunset: the sun 'goes over' the ridge — 산 너머로 넘어가다.
examples: 다음 문제로 넘어가요.
Let's move on to the next question.
Simple; 으로 marks the next item — a classroom/meeting staple.
이번 실수는 그냥 넘어갈게요.
I'll let this mistake slide this time.
Everyday, idiomatic; 그냥 넘어가다 = overlook, with -ㄹ게요 (I will).
해가 산 너머로 넘어가니 금방 어두워졌어요.
Once the sun dipped behind the mountain, it got dark fast.
Real-situation; 산 너머로 (over the ridge) + 넘어가다 = the sun setting.
nuance: 넘어가다 is 넘다 (to cross/exceed) + 가다 (go): literally to go over something — a hill, wall, or ridge — to the other side, and figuratively to 'move on' to the next page, topic, or step (다음으로 넘어가다), which makes it a fixture in lessons and meetings. Watch three layers English speakers blur: the physical obstacle takes 를/을 (산을 넘어가다), the next item takes 으로/로 (다음으로 넘어가다), and the idiom 그냥 넘어가다 means to let something slide / overlook it. It also fixes the sunset image, 해가 넘어가다. The dangerous near-look-alike is 넘어지다 ('to fall over, topple') — one letter apart but a totally different action — and don't confuse it with the transitive 넘기다 ('to flip/hand over/get past'). For simply going somewhere, 가다 suffices; 넘어가다 specifically adds the 'over/across or onward' nuance. The pitfall is the 넘어가다/넘어지다 mix-up and choosing the wrong particle for obstacle vs next-step.

Using the wrong particle: an obstacle takes 를/을 (산을 넘어가다) but the next step takes 으로 (다음으로 넘어가다).
Mixing it with transitive 넘기다 — you 페이지를 넘기다 (flip a page) but 다음 페이지로 넘어가다 (move on to the next page).

usage: 으로 marks the direction you rotate toward; core for giving directions.
바퀴 is the counter for laps/loops: 한 바퀴, 두 바퀴 돌다.
Figurative: rumors/colds/money 'circulate' — subject takes 이/가 (소문이 돌아요).
Idiom: 머리가/정신이 돌다 = head spins; mildly slangy, use with care.
examples: 여기서 왼쪽으로 도세요.
Turn left here.
Simple direction-giving; the ㄹ drops in the polite request → 도세요.
운동장을 한 바퀴 돌았어요.
I went around the track once.
Everyday; 를 marks the loop's path, 한 바퀴 counts the lap.
요즘 회사에 이상한 소문이 돌고 있어요.
A strange rumor is going around the office these days.
Real-situation, figurative; 소문이 돌다 (subject + 이/가), -고 있다 = ongoing.
nuance: 돌다 means to turn, spin, or go around, and intransitively to circulate (소문/돈/감기가 돌다 = rumors/money/a cold going around). It is a ㄹ-stem (ㄹ-탈락) verb, which is the main hurdle: the ㄹ vanishes before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal is 돕니다 (not 돌습니다) and the polite 'please turn' for directions is 도세요 (not 돌으세요), while the 어-form is the regular 돌아요. The crucial pair English speakers must split is 돌다 vs 돌리다: 돌다 is intransitive (something turns/spins by itself — 팽이가 돌다, the wheel turns), whereas 돌리다 is transitive (you turn something — 핸들을 돌리다). Direction takes 으로 (오른쪽으로 돌다); a lap takes the counter 바퀴. The pitfall is regularizing the ㄹ-stem forms and using 돌다 where you actually act on an object, which needs 돌리다.

usage: 를 marks the thing turned (body part); 고개를 돌리다 = look/turn away.
Operating a control by rotating it; the transitive partner of 돌다.
Figurative: 마음을 돌리다 = win someone over / turn a heart around.
examples: 고개를 왼쪽으로 돌렸어요.
I turned my head to the left.
Simple; 를 (object) + 으로 (direction) — you act on 고개.
자기 전에 세탁기를 돌렸어요.
I ran the washing machine before bed.
Everyday household phrase; 돌리다 = operate the machine.
끝까지 설득해서 결국 그 사람 마음을 돌렸어요.
I kept persuading and finally changed that person's mind.
Real-situation, figurative; 마음을 돌리다 = win them over.
nuance: 돌리다 is the transitive partner of 돌다 (built with the causative -리-): you turn something — a handle, your head — or 'run' a machine like a washer or vacuum (세탁기를 돌리다). It is a regular 이-stem verb, so the 어-form is simply 돌려요 / 돌렸어요 with no ㄹ-drop drama, unlike its intransitive sibling 돌다. It also carries rich idioms: 마음을 돌리다 (change someone's mind / win them over), 고개를 돌리다 (turn away), 전화를 돌리다 (older: dial / route a call). The object always takes 를/을. The pitfall is reaching for 돌다 when an object is involved, and over-applying ㄹ-stem rules that simply don't apply here.

english: to set out / to step forward
usage: 를/을 marks the place left behind; 집을 나서다 = head out to start the day.
to set out on one's way
길을 나서다 = hit the road; flavor of beginning a journey.
으로 marks direction; physically advancing or volunteering to the front.
to throw oneself in / pitch in actively
Idiom: 'roll up sleeves'; 나서다 here = volunteer eagerly to help.
examples: 아침 일찍 집을 나섰어요.
I set out from home early in the morning.
Simple; 집을 나서다 takes 를/을 — leaving home to start the day.
발표하겠다고 한 걸음 앞으로 나섰어요.
I stepped forward to volunteer to present.
Everyday; 앞으로 나서다 = step up/forward to take something on.
이웃들이 직접 문제 해결에 나섰어요.
The neighbors took it on themselves to solve the problem.
Real-situation, figurative; -에 나서다 = step up to undertake a task.
nuance: 나서다 is 나다/나- ('come out') + 서다 (stand/step), giving two linked senses: to set out / head off (집을 나서다 = leave home to start your day; 길을 나서다 = hit the road) and to step forward — physically to the front, or figuratively to volunteer and take charge (문제 해결에 나서다 = step up to tackle a problem). The line versus plain 나가다 ('go out') matters: 나가다 just exits a space, while 나서다 carries the flavor of launching a journey or actively putting yourself forward, often with initiative or even pushiness — note 나서다 can imply meddling, as in 남의 일에 나서다 (butt into others' business). For leaving home, 집을 나서다 takes the object marker 를/을, where 나가다 would too but sounds plainer. Idioms like 발 벗고 나서다 (pitch in wholeheartedly) live here. The pitfall is treating it as a flat synonym of 나가다 and missing the 'take the initiative' nuance.

Using 에 for the place left: it is 집을 나서다 (를/을), not 집에 나서다.
Overusing 나서다 for 'help out' without noticing its 'put yourself forward' tone — 남의 일에 나서다 can sound like meddling.

english: to run into / to bump into
usage: 우연히 (by chance) is the natural partner; underlines the unplanned meeting.
Set phrase; the eyes are the subject (눈이), so it takes 이/가, not 를.
to come face to face with
The other party can take 와/과 (…와 마주치다) as well as the 를/을 object.
to run into (someone) on the street
에서 marks the place of the chance encounter.
examples: 길에서 친구를 마주쳤어요.
I ran into a friend on the street.
Simple; the person met takes 를/을, 에서 marks the place.
엘리베이터에서 우연히 선생님을 마주쳤어요.
I happened to run into my teacher in the elevator.
Everyday; 우연히 (by chance) makes the accidental nature explicit.
복도에서 그 사람과 눈이 마주쳐서 어색했어요.
Our eyes met in the hallway and it was awkward.
Real-situation; 눈이 마주치다 (subject + 이/가) + -아서 (so, as a result).
nuance: 마주치다 is 마주 ('facing, head-on') + 치다 ('strike'), literally 'to strike facing each other', i.e. to run/bump into someone or something unexpectedly, by chance. The person you encounter takes 를/을 (친구를 마주치다) or the comitative 와/과 (친구와 마주치다), and it is the fixed phrase for eye contact, 눈이 마주치다 — where the eyes are the subject with 이/가, a structure English speakers often get wrong by saying 눈을 마주쳤어요. The key contrast is with 만나다 ('to meet'): 만나다 covers planned, intended meetings (친구를 만나다 = meet up with a friend on purpose), while 마주치다 is strictly accidental and momentary, hence its frequent companion 우연히 (by chance). Compare also 부딪치다, the more physical 'collide/crash into' (사람과 부딪치다 = literally bump bodies). The pitfall is using 마주치다 for an arranged get-together, and mis-marking the eye-contact phrase with 를 instead of 이/가.
